questions.question_text: A 28-year-old is brought to the emergency department after using cocaine. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of action of cocaine?

options.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine
Direct agonism at dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum
Inhibition of monoamine oxidase, preventing dopamine breakdown
Release of dopamine from vesicular stores in presynaptic neurons
Blockade of the norepinephrine transporter (NET) only, with no effect on dopamine

correct_answer.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine

questions.explanation: Cocaine blocks the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), preventing reuptake of dopamine from the synapse. This leads to accumulation of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic pathway), producing euphoria. Unlike amphetamines, cocaine does not cause active release of dopamine from vesicular stores. Reference: Stahl SM, Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology (5th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: A forensic psychiatrist explains how amphetamine differs from cocaine in producing stimulant effects. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of action of amphetamine?

options.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter without affecting vesicular release
Direct agonism at postsynaptic dopamine D1 and D2 receptors
Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores
Inhibition of catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), reducing dopamine degradation
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibition with secondary dopamine release

correct_answer.text: Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores

questions.explanation: Amphetamine enters presynaptic neurons via the DAT and reverses its direction of transport, causing efflux of dopamine into the synapse. It also displaces dopamine from vesicular storage (via VMAT2 inhibition) and inhibits MAO. This mechanism of active dopamine release distinguishes it from cocaine. Reference: Nestler EJ et al., Molecular Neuropharmacology (3rd ed.), McGraw-Hill, 2015.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman overdosed on zopiclone. The clinician considers using flumazenil. Which of the following best describes how flumazenil reverses the effects of zopiclone?

options.text: It acts as a GABA-A positive allosteric modulator, competing with zopiclone at the benzodiazepine binding site
It competitively antagonises zopiclone at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors, reducing chloride influx
It directly blocks chloride channels, preventing chloride influx regardless of GABA binding
It increases the breakdown of zopiclone through induction of CYP3A4 enzymes
It acts as an inverse agonist at GABA-A receptors, reversing all sedative effects permanently

correct_answer.text: It competitively antagonises zopiclone at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors, reducing chloride influx

questions.explanation: Flumazenil competitively antagonises benzodiazepines and zopiclone at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors, preventing chloride influx and reversing sedation. It is not an inverse agonist and does not directly block chloride channels. Reference: BNF. Rang HP et al. Rang and Dale's Pharmacology (9th ed.), 2019.

questions.question_text: A patient on clozapine abruptly stops smoking. Two weeks later his clozapine plasma levels are significantly elevated. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.text: Increased absorption of clozapine from the gastrointestinal tract after smoking cessation
De-induction of CYP1A2 following removal of tobacco smoke polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
Increased renal clearance of clozapine metabolites after smoking cessation
Nicotine directly inhibits the metabolism of clozapine via CYP3A4
Smoking cessation increases plasma protein binding of clozapine, reducing free drug clearance

correct_answer.text: De-induction of CYP1A2 following removal of tobacco smoke polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons

questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (not nicotine) induce CYP1A2, the primary enzyme metabolising clozapine. Abrupt smoking cessation removes this induction (de-induction), decreasing clearance and raising plasma levels. The same applies to olanzapine. Reference: Taylor D et al. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (14th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: A consultant psychiatrist discusses deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression. Which brain target is most commonly used?
questions.explanation: The subgenual cingulate cortex (area 25) is the most widely studied DBS target for treatment-resistant depression, identified by Mayberg and colleagues as a hub of limbic-cortical dysregulation. Reference: Mayberg HS et al. Neuron 2005;45:651-660.

questions.question_text: A neuroscientist studying circadian rhythm regulation asks which serotonin receptor subtype is specifically implicated in circadian modulation. Which receptor is this?
questions.explanation: The 5-HT7 receptor plays a key role in circadian rhythm regulation. It is expressed in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and modulates circadian phase. Drugs with 5-HT7 antagonism (agomelatine, lurasidone) influence circadian rhythms. Reference: Hedlund PB. Psychopharmacology 2009;206:345-354.

questions.question_text: A pharmacology lecturer asks students to identify which of the following is a metabotropic (G-protein coupled) receptor. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: The 5-HT2A receptor is a Gq-coupled metabotropic (GPCR) receptor. NMDA, GABA-A, 5-HT3, and nicotinic receptors are all ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels). Reference: Stahl SM, Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology (5th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: Which dopaminergic pathway is primarily responsible for reward, motivation, and reinforcement learning?
questions.explanation: The mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway (VTA to nucleus accumbens) is the primary neural substrate of reward and reinforcement. It is dysregulated in substance dependence and psychosis. Reference: Koob GF, Volkow ND. Lancet Psychiatry 2016;3:760-773.

questions.question_text: During a clozapine prescribing workshop, a trainee asks about the risk of agranulocytosis. Which best reflects the approximate lifetime risk of clozapine-induced agranulocytosis?
questions.explanation: The lifetime risk of clozapine-induced agranulocytosis (ANC <500/mm³) is approximately 1% (0.5-1%). Mandatory haematological monitoring is required. Reference: Taylor D et al. Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (14th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: Which anticonvulsant is most associated with anorexia and weight loss?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is the anticonvulsant most consistently associated with anorexia and weight loss, via modulation of hypothalamic appetite-regulating circuits and AMPA receptor blockade. In contrast, valproate and gabapentin cause weight gain. Reference: Stahl SM. Prescriber's Guide (7th ed.), 2020.

questions.question_text: Which of the following hypnotics has the shortest elimination half-life?
questions.explanation: Zolpidem has a half-life of approximately 2-3 hours (shortest among options listed). Temazepam: 8-15h; Oxazepam: 5-15h; Nitrazepam: 16-48h; Diazepam: 20-100h. Reference: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (14th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: Caffeine's stimulant properties are mediated through which receptor mechanism?

options.text: Agonism at dopamine D1 receptors in the prefrontal cortex
Blockade of GABA-A receptors, reducing inhibitory tone
Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase, increasing intracellular cAMP
Agonism at alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, increasing arousal

correct_answer.text: Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors

questions.explanation: Caffeine competitively antagonises adenosine A1 and A2A receptors. Adenosine accumulates during wakefulness and promotes sleep; blocking it promotes alertness. Reference: Fredholm BB et al. Pharmacol Rev 1999;51:83-133.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes buprenorphine's mechanism of action?

options.text: Full agonist at mu-opioid receptors and antagonist at delta-opioid receptors
Partial agonist at mu-opioid receptors and antagonist at kappa-opioid receptors
Full antagonist at all opioid receptor subtypes (mu, kappa, delta)
Full agonist at both mu and kappa-opioid receptors
Partial agonist at kappa-opioid receptors with no activity at mu receptors

correct_answer.text: Partial agonist at mu-opioid receptors and antagonist at kappa-opioid receptors

questions.explanation: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu-opioid receptors (with a ceiling effect for respiratory depression) and an antagonist at kappa-opioid receptors. Its high affinity blocks other opioids. Reference: Stahl SM, Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology (5th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes memantine's mechanism of action?

options.text: Reversible inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase, increasing synaptic acetylcholine
Competitive antagonist at AMPA glutamate receptors
Non-competitive antagonist at NMDA glutamate receptors
Partial agonist at muscarinic M1 receptors
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor with secondary glutamate modulation

correct_answer.text: Non-competitive antagonist at NMDA glutamate receptors

questions.explanation: Memantine is an uncompetitive (non-competitive, voltage-dependent) NMDA-receptor antagonist. It blocks tonically over-activated NMDA receptors (reducing excitotoxicity) while preserving physiological phasic activation. Reference: Lipton SA. Nature Rev Drug Discov 2006;5:160-170.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes lamotrigine's primary mechanism of action?

options.text: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors
Blockade of the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels

questions.explanation: Lamotrigine primarily exerts use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels (preferentially in the inactivated state), reducing pre-synaptic glutamate release. Reference: Ketter TA et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2003;64(Suppl 8):10-21.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes pregabalin's primary mechanism of action?

options.text: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors, increasing chloride influx
Blockade of the alpha-2-delta (α2δ) subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels
Competitive antagonism at NMDA glutamate receptors
Selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition

correct_answer.text: Blockade of the alpha-2-delta (α2δ) subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels

questions.explanation: Pregabalin binds to the alpha-2-delta (α2δ) auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing calcium influx at presynaptic terminals and decreasing release of excitatory neurotransmitters. Despite its GABA-like structure, it has no direct GABAergic activity. Reference: Stahl SM, Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology (5th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: To reverse the psychedelic effects of psilocybin, which receptor must be blocked?
questions.explanation: Psilocybin's psychedelic effects are mediated via 5-HT2A agonism in cortical pyramidal neurons. The 5-HT2A antagonist ketanserin reverses these effects in experimental studies. All classical psychedelics act via 5-HT2A agonism. Reference: Nichols DE. Pharmacol Rev 2016;68:264-355.

questions.question_text: A student asks about the mechanism of bupropion. Which of the following correctly describes it?

options.text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibition with additional norepinephrine reuptake inhibition
Norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibition (NDRI) without significant serotonin effects
Monoamine oxidase A inhibition, preventing serotonin and norepinephrine breakdown
Serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibition with strong 5-HT2A antagonism
Partial agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors plus dopamine reuptake inhibition

correct_answer.text: Norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibition (NDRI) without significant serotonin effects

questions.explanation: Bupropion is a norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) with minimal serotonin transporter activity. This differentiates it from SSRIs and SNRIs. Its dopaminergic mechanism supports its use in smoking cessation. Reference: Stahl SM et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2004;65:182-192.

questions.question_text: Which ion primarily triggers neurotransmitter release from synaptic vesicles via exocytosis?
questions.explanation: Calcium (Ca²⁺) influx through voltage-gated calcium channels at presynaptic terminals triggers SNARE-complex-mediated vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release. Drugs blocking presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels (gabapentin, pregabalin) thereby reduce neurotransmitter release. Reference: Kandel ER et al. Principles of Neural Science (6th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes vortioxetine's mechanism of action?

options.text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibition only, with no receptor activity
Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition with strong D2 antagonism
Multimodal serotonergic action: SERT inhibition plus 5-HT3/7 antagonism and 5-HT1A partial agonism
Partial agonist at 5-HT1A receptors and full antagonist at 5-HT2A receptors only

correct_answer.text: Multimodal serotonergic action: SERT inhibition plus 5-HT3/7 antagonism and 5-HT1A partial agonism

questions.explanation: Vortioxetine is a multimodal antidepressant: SERT inhibition, 5-HT3, 5-HT7 antagonism, 5-HT1A partial agonism, 5-HT1B antagonism, 5-HT1D agonism. This combination produces pro-cognitive effects beyond SERT inhibition alone. Reference: Sanchez C et al. Neuropharmacology 2015;71:352-363.

questions.question_text: A teacher notices a child can solve a problem with adult guidance but not independently. What is the term for the distance between a child's independent performance and what they can achieve with guidance?
questions.explanation: Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) describes the gap between independent ability and what can be achieved with guidance. Scaffolding refers to the support provided within the ZPD. Reference: Vygotsky LS. Mind in Society. Harvard University Press, 1978.

questions.question_text: A woman has satisfying family relationships and close friendships. According to Maslow's hierarchy, what is the next stage she would be motivated to fulfil?
questions.explanation: Maslow's Hierarchy (bottom to top): Physiological → Safety → Love and Belonging → Esteem → Self-actualisation. Once love/belonging needs are met, esteem needs (achievement, recognition, respect) become the motivating force. Reference: Maslow AH. Psychol Rev 1943;50:370-396.

questions.question_text: According to Erikson\'s psychosocial theory, a 4-year-old child is at which stage?
questions.explanation: A 4-year-old is in Erikson\'s Initiative vs Guilt stage (ages 3-6 years). Children assert themselves and take initiative; healthy resolution leads to purposefulness. Key virtue: purpose. Reference: Erikson EH. Childhood and Society. Norton, 1950.

questions.question_text: An adolescent has committed to values and beliefs without going through a period of exploration. According to Marcia's identity status theory, this is which identity status?
questions.explanation: Foreclosure (Marcia) describes commitment to an identity without prior exploration or crisis - typically adopting parental values without questioning them. Reference: Marcia JE. J Pers Soc Psychol 1966;3:551-558.

questions.question_text: Which language milestone is typically achieved by age 13?
questions.explanation: By age 13, children typically have a vocabulary of approximately 20,000 words. Vocabulary expands rapidly during school years. Reference: Owens RE. Language Development (9th ed.), Pearson, 2016.

questions.question_text: Which language achievement is typically expected by age 5?

options.text: Understanding of passive voice constructions (passive speech)

correct_answer.text: Understanding of passive voice constructions (passive speech)

questions.explanation: By age 5, children can understand passive voice constructions. They have approximately 2,000-2,500 words and produce sentences of 5-6 words. Reference: Owens RE. Language Development (9th ed.), Pearson, 2016.

questions.question_text: From adolescence to adulthood, which of the following best describes brain developmental changes?

options.text: Increase in grey matter and decrease in white matter
Decrease in grey matter and increase in white matter
Increase in both grey matter and white matter
Decrease in both grey matter and white matter
Grey matter remains stable while white matter decreases

correct_answer.text: Decrease in grey matter and increase in white matter

questions.explanation: From adolescence to adulthood, grey matter decreases (synaptic pruning) while white matter increases (progressive myelination). These processes continue into the mid-20s, corresponding to improvements in executive function. Reference: Giedd JN et al. Nat Neurosci 1999;2:861-863.

questions.question_text: Twin studies examining psychological traits have shown which trait to have the highest heritability?
questions.explanation: General intelligence (IQ) has among the highest heritability of any psychological trait, with estimates of 50-80% in adults from twin studies. Reference: Plomin R et al. Perspect Psychol Sci 2016;11:3-23.

questions.question_text: A teacher gives a lecture on the risks of early sexual relationships. A student decides not to engage in sexual relationships. Which concept best explains this change?

options.text: Cognitive attitude change through persuasive communication

correct_answer.text: Cognitive attitude change through persuasive communication

questions.explanation: This is cognitive attitude change through persuasive communication - the student has received information that changes her beliefs and intentions. This is a social psychology/cognitive learning concept, not simple operant conditioning. Reference: Ajzen I, Fishbein M. Understanding Attitudes and Predicting Social Behaviour. 1980.

questions.question_text: According to the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Personality Disorders, a personality disorder characterised by emotional lability, anxiousness, and separation insecurity involves which higher-order personality trait domain?
questions.explanation: Negative affectivity encompasses emotional lability, anxiousness, separation insecurity, submissiveness, and depressivity. It is the relevant AMPD domain. Reference: DSM-5, APA, 2013.

questions.question_text: A newborn animal forms an attachment to the first moving object it encounters, in an irreversible process occurring within a narrow time window. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Imprinting is rapid, early learning that occurs during a critical period, studied by Konrad Lorenz in greylag geese. It is distinguished by: restriction to a critical period, irreversibility, and no requirement for reinforcement. Reference: Lorenz KZ. J Ornithol 1935;83:137-413.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most accurate statement about positive and negative reinforcement?

options.text: Positive reinforcement decreases behaviour by adding a pleasant stimulus
Negative reinforcement decreases behaviour by removing an aversive stimulus
Positive reinforcement increases behaviour by adding a pleasant stimulus; negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing an aversive stimulus
Positive reinforcement and negative reinforcement both decrease the frequency of behaviour
Negative reinforcement involves adding an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour

correct_answer.text: Positive reinforcement increases behaviour by adding a pleasant stimulus; negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing an aversive stimulus

questions.explanation: Both positive and negative reinforcement increase the frequency of a behaviour. Positive reinforcement adds a reward; negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus. Both are distinct from punishment (which decreases behaviour). Reference: Skinner BF. The Behavior of Organisms. 1938.

questions.question_text: A child watches an older sibling share toys and subsequently begins sharing without being directly rewarded. This is an example of which type of learning?
questions.explanation: Observational learning (modelling, social learning) occurs when behaviours are acquired by watching others without direct reinforcement. Developed by Bandura (Bobo doll experiments). Reference: Bandura A. Social Learning Theory. 1977.

questions.question_text: A child encounters a 'cat' and modifies her existing 'dog' schema to incorporate this new information. What is the term for modifying an existing schema to accommodate new information?
questions.explanation: Accommodation (Piaget) is modifying or creating a new schema to incorporate information that cannot fit into existing schemas. In contrast, assimilation incorporates new information into existing schemas without modifying them. Reference: Piaget J. The Origins of Intelligence in Children. 1952.

questions.question_text: A young child calls all adult males 'Daddy' — incorporating new people into an existing mental category without modifying the category. What is this Piagetian process?
questions.explanation: Assimilation (Piaget) incorporates new information into existing schemas without modifying them. The complementary process, accommodation, modifies schemas for new information. Reference: Piaget J. The Language and Thought of the Child. 1926.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old in foster care does not seek comfort from the carer when distressed, shows no preference for the carer over strangers, and appears emotionally withdrawn. Which diagnosis is most consistent?
questions.explanation: Reactive attachment disorder (inhibited type) is characterised by markedly disturbed attachment behaviours — rarely seeking comfort, minimal social responsiveness, limited positive affect — resulting from severe social neglect. Reference: DSM-5, ICD-11.

questions.question_text: The prelinguistic phase of communication development is characteristically prolonged in which neurodevelopmental condition?
questions.explanation: Prelinguistic deficits (reduced joint attention, limited pointing, delayed babbling) are early developmental markers of ASD and are core diagnostic targets for early intervention. Reference: Lord C et al. Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020;6:5.

questions.question_text: A toddler shows mild negative mood in new situations, slow adaptability, and low intensity of reactions but eventually adjusts. Which temperament category is this?
questions.explanation: Thomas and Chess's slow-to-warm-up temperament: initially withdrawn in novelty, slowly adapts, low intensity reactions. Differs from difficult temperament (intense reactions). Reference: Thomas A, Chess S. Temperament and Development, 1977.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes social capital?

options.text: The financial assets available to a community for mental health services
The level of formal education attained within a community
Social networks, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action and mutual benefit
The physical infrastructure supporting social interaction
Individual socioeconomic status as measured by income and occupation

correct_answer.text: Social networks, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action and mutual benefit

questions.explanation: Social capital (Putnam, Bourdieu) refers to social networks, norms of reciprocity, and trust that facilitate cooperation for mutual benefit. High social capital is associated with better mental health outcomes. Reference: Putnam RD. Bowling Alone. 2000.

questions.question_text: In the Camberwell Family Interview, which component is specifically measured as part of expressed emotion?

options.text: Critical comments made by family members about the patient
Number of psychiatric admissions in the past year

correct_answer.text: Critical comments made by family members about the patient

questions.explanation: The Camberwell Family Interview measures Expressed Emotion (EE) including critical comments, hostility, emotional over-involvement, warmth, and positive remarks. High EE predicts relapse in schizophrenia, depression, and bipolar disorder. Reference: Leff J, Vaughn C. Expressed Emotion in Families. 1985.

questions.question_text: Which type of memory is least affected in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Procedural memory (stored in basal ganglia/cerebellum) is the least affected in schizophrenia. Working memory (prefrontal cortex) is classically impaired, as are episodic memory, attention, and processing speed. Reference: Aleman A et al. Am J Psychiatry 1999;156:1358-1366.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive ability is least affected by normal ageing?
questions.explanation: Procedural memory is among the most resistant cognitive functions to normal ageing. Normal ageing primarily affects processing speed, working memory, divided attention, and new episodic memory encoding. Reference: Park DC, Reuter-Lorenz P. Annu Rev Psychol 2009;60:173-196.

questions.question_text: Which memory task shows the least decline with normal ageing?

options.text: Free recall of a word list

questions.explanation: Simple recognition tasks show the least decline with normal ageing. Recognition requires only familiarity judgements and places fewer demands on effortful retrieval (which declines with age). Reference: Light LL. Annu Rev Psychol 1991;42:333-376.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive domain does digit span primarily measure?
questions.explanation: Digit span (forward and backward) is the most widely used measure of verbal working memory/phonological loop capacity. Normal forward digit span is 7±2 digits. Reference: Baddeley AD. Working Memory. Clarendon Press, 1986.

questions.question_text: Which assessment task most directly measures motor speed?
questions.explanation: The finger tapping test (finger oscillation test) directly measures motor speed and fine motor dexterity. It is part of the Halstead-Reitan Battery. Reference: Reitan RM, Wolfson D. The Halstead-Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery. 1985.

questions.question_text: A patient must sort cards by rules that change without warning, requiring flexible strategy shifting. Which test is this?
questions.explanation: The WCST assesses cognitive flexibility, set-shifting, and abstract reasoning. Perseverative errors are the hallmark of frontal lobe dysfunction. Reference: Milner B. Arch Neurol 1963;9:90-100.

questions.question_text: Digital phenotyping uses passively collected smartphone sensor data to track psychiatric symptoms. Which combination of data streams has been most studied for detecting and predicting depressive episode onset?
questions.explanation: Digital phenotyping passively collects behavioural data from smartphone sensors to generate continuous, objective measures of psychiatric state. The most studied data streams for depression include: GPS (location variability, mobility, time at home, circadian movement patterns); communication patterns (call/text frequency, social network diversity — reduced in depression); screen time (total usage, app type — social isolation patterns); accelerometry/actigraphy (physical activity, sleep-wake cycles, step count). Machine learning algorithms combining these streams predict depressive episodes with AUCs of 0.80–0.90 in research settings. Key validated tools include AWARE framework, Beiwe platform, and commercial wearables. Clinical translation challenges include: privacy and consent, data security, algorithm fairness across populations, reimbursement models, and integrating digital biomarkers into clinical workflows. The concept of 'digital biomarkers' extends beyond smartphones to wearables monitoring heart rate variability (HRV — inversely correlated with depressive and anxiety states), galvanic skin response, and sleep architecture (actigraphy).

questions.question_text: The Hayling sentence completion test primarily measures which executive function?
questions.explanation: The Hayling test measures response initiation (Part A: sensible sentence completion) and response suppression (Part B: unrelated word). Suppression deficits are associated with frontal lobe impairment. Reference: Burgess PW, Shallice T. The Hayling and Brixton Tests. 1997.

questions.question_text: A patient provides a detailed account of what he had for breakfast, including who was present and where he was. Which type of memory is this testing?
questions.explanation: Episodic memory stores personally experienced events with their spatiotemporal context - the 'what, where, and when' of personal experience. It is highly vulnerable to hippocampal damage and impaired early in Alzheimer's. Reference: Tulving E. Annu Rev Psychol 2002;53:1-25.

questions.question_text: When asked 'What is breakfast?' a patient with amnesia correctly explains it is the first meal of the day. What type of memory enables this?
questions.explanation: Semantic memory stores general world knowledge — facts, concepts, and word meanings — independent of personal experience. It is encoded in lateral/inferior temporal lobes and is more resistant to hippocampal damage than episodic memory. Reference: Tulving E, Markowitsch HJ. Hippocampus 1998;8:198-204.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive test most specifically evaluates abstract thinking?
questions.explanation: The Similarities subtest assesses abstract thinking — identifying categorical/conceptual relationships between objects. It is included in the WAIS and MMSE. Concrete responses indicate lower abstraction. Reference: Wechsler D. WAIS-IV. Pearson, 2008.

questions.question_text: Which brain lobe and area are most consistently activated during auditory verbal hallucinations?

options.text: Temporal lobe – superior temporal gyrus (Heschl's gyrus/Wernicke's area)

correct_answer.text: Temporal lobe – superior temporal gyrus (Heschl's gyrus/Wernicke's area)

questions.explanation: Auditory verbal hallucinations are most consistently associated with activation of the superior temporal gyrus (including Heschl's gyrus and Wernicke's area). Reduced grey matter in the STG correlates with AVH frequency in schizophrenia. Reference: Allen P et al. Neurosci Lett 2008;14:484-498.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a component of the hippocampal formation?
questions.explanation: The hippocampal formation consists of the dentate gyrus, Ammon's horn (CA1-CA4), and the subiculum. The dentate gyrus is one of the few regions capable of adult neurogenesis and plays a role in pattern separation. Reference: Amaral DG, Lavenex P. The Hippocampus Book. Oxford University Press, 2007.

questions.question_text: Which brain region is the last to reach full maturational development?

options.text: Anterior pole of the frontal lobe (prefrontal cortex)

correct_answer.text: Anterior pole of the frontal lobe (prefrontal cortex)

questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex matures last, with myelination and synaptic pruning continuing into the mid-20s. This explains the relative immaturity of executive function and impulse control in adolescents. Reference: Casey BJ et al. Ann NY Acad Sci 2008;1124:111-126.

questions.question_text: From which primary germ layer does the neural crest originate?
questions.explanation: The neural crest originates from the ectoderm (neuroectoderm at the dorsal margins of the neural plate). Neural crest cells give rise to the peripheral nervous system, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and craniofacial cartilage. Reference: Sadock BJ et al. Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook (10th ed.), 2017.

questions.question_text: In right-handed individuals, which brain structure shows a larger left hemisphere, corresponding to language lateralisation?

options.text: Heschl's gyrus and the planum temporale

correct_answer.text: Heschl's gyrus and the planum temporale

questions.explanation: The planum temporale (posterior STG, within Sylvian fissure, posterior to Heschl's gyrus) is larger in the left hemisphere in ~65% of right-handed people - a structural asymmetry corresponding to language lateralisation. First described by Geschwind and Levitsky (1968). Reference: Geschwind N, Levitsky W. Science 1968;161:186-187.

questions.question_text: From which primary embryological brain division do the epithalamus and thalamus develop?
questions.explanation: The thalamus and epithalamus develop from the diencephalon, which derives from the prosencephalon (forebrain). The telencephalon develops into the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and hippocampus. Reference: Sadock BJ et al. Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook (10th ed.), 2017.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes descriptive psychopathology?

options.text: Explanation of abnormal experiences using biological and psychological mechanisms
Systematic description of abnormal experiences from the patient's subjective perspective, without presupposing causation
Statistical study of the prevalence of mental disorder in populations
Classification of mental disorders according to operational diagnostic criteria
Neuroimaging correlation of psychiatric symptoms with brain abnormalities

correct_answer.text: Systematic description of abnormal experiences from the patient's subjective perspective, without presupposing causation

questions.explanation: Descriptive psychopathology (Jaspers) systematically describes abnormal psychological experiences as subjectively experienced by the patient — the phenomena themselves, without explaining their causes. It uses the phenomenological method. Reference: Jaspers K. General Psychopathology. Johns Hopkins University Press, 1963.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a primary structural component of the blood-brain barrier (BBB)?

options.text: Tight junctions between cerebrovascular endothelial cells
Basal lamina of the capillary endothelium

questions.explanation: The BBB is formed by: cerebrovascular endothelial cells with tight junctions (primary barrier), astrocyte end-feet, pericytes, and basal lamina. ApoE is a lipoprotein involved in Alzheimer's risk but is not a structural BBB component. Reference: Zlokovic BV. Neuron 2008;57:178-201.

questions.question_text: Which neuroimaging technique does NOT require an MRI scanner?
questions.explanation: EEG measures electrical brain activity through scalp electrodes and does not use an MRI scanner. DTI, fMRI, VBM, and structural MRI all require MRI scanners. PET and SPECT also do not use MRI scanners. Reference: Sadock BJ et al. Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook (10th ed.), 2017.

questions.question_text: Which MRI-based technique quantifies white matter tract integrity and density?
questions.explanation: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures anisotropic water diffusion along white matter tracts. Fractional anisotropy (FA) quantifies tract integrity; reduced FA indicates axonal loss or demyelination. Tractography reconstructs 3D fibre pathways. Reference: Basser PJ, Pierpaoli C. J Magn Reson 1996;111:209-219.

questions.question_text: Which CSF biomarker is characteristically decreased in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: CSF Aβ42 is decreased in Alzheimer's because it is sequestered into amyloid plaques, reducing efflux into CSF. Total tau and p-tau are increased; 14-3-3 protein is elevated in CJD. Reference: Jack CR et al. Alzheimers Dement 2018;14:535-562.

questions.question_text: Which protein is the primary disease-specific biomarker currently under investigation for Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: Mutant huntingtin protein (mHTT) is the disease-specific biomarker for Huntington's disease, measurable in blood and CSF using ultra-sensitive assays. Rising levels predict proximity to clinical onset. Reference: Wild EJ et al. J Clin Invest 2015;125:1979-1986.

questions.question_text: Which protein is the primary component of Lewy bodies in dementia with Lewy bodies?
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies are composed primarily of aggregated, misfolded alpha-synuclein. DLB, Parkinson's disease, and PD-dementia are alpha-synucleinopathies. Reference: McKeith IG et al. Neurology 2017;89:88-100.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old woman presents with flu-like illness, then psychiatric symptoms, movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesias, catatonia), and seizures. Anti-NMDA receptor antibodies are found in CSF. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with prodromal flu-like illness, psychiatric symptoms, movement disorder, seizures, and autonomic instability. Predominantly young women, associated with ovarian teratoma in ~50%. CSF anti-GluN1 antibodies are diagnostic. Reference: Dalmau J et al. Ann Neurol 2007;61:25-36.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with limbic encephalitis, faciobrachial dystonic seizures, progressive amnesia, and hyponatremia. Which antibody is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: LGI1 encephalitis is characterised by faciobrachial dystonic seizures, limbic encephalitis with subacute memory impairment, and hyponatremia. Mostly affects older adults, more common in men. Reference: Lai M et al. Ann Neurol 2010;67:341-352.

questions.question_text: The 'pulvinar sign' on MRI brain is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: The pulvinar sign — bilateral high signal in posterior thalami on T2/FLAIR MRI — is characteristic of vCJD. It presents in younger patients with early psychiatric symptoms, progressing to ataxia and cognitive decline. Reference: Zeidler M et al. Lancet 2000;355:1412-1418.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a recognised human prion disease?
questions.explanation: Fatal familial insomnia (FFI) is a prion disease caused by a PRNP gene mutation (D178N). It causes progressive untreatable insomnia, autonomic dysfunction, and motor symptoms. Other prion diseases include CJD, Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker, and Kuru. Reference: Montagna P et al. Sleep Med Rev 2003;7:133-142.

questions.question_text: Which vaccine has been associated with a significantly reduced risk of developing dementia in large population studies?
questions.explanation: Large population-based studies show herpes zoster vaccination is associated with ~20% reduced dementia risk. Herpes viruses (HSV-1, VZV) are implicated in Alzheimer's pathogenesis via neuroinflammation and amyloid production. Reference: Eyting M et al. Nature 2024;629.

questions.question_text: What is the most important adverse effect to monitor for with lecanemab (anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody)?
questions.explanation: ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities) including oedema (ARIA-E) and microhaemorrhages (ARIA-H) are the most important adverse effects of lecanemab. They occurred in ~35% in the CLARITY AD trial. Regular MRI monitoring is required. Reference: van Dyck CH et al. N Engl J Med 2023;388:9-21.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the key difference between thought insertion and thought broadcast?

options.text: Thought insertion involves thoughts leaving the patient's mind; thought broadcast involves external thoughts being placed in
Thought insertion involves external thoughts being placed into the patient's mind; thought broadcast involves the patient's thoughts being transmitted to others
Thought insertion is a negative symptom; thought broadcast is a positive symptom
Thought insertion is specific to schizophrenia; thought broadcast occurs only in mania
Thought insertion involves hearing thoughts aloud; thought broadcast involves thought withdrawal

correct_answer.text: Thought insertion involves external thoughts being placed into the patient's mind; thought broadcast involves the patient's thoughts being transmitted to others

questions.explanation: Thought insertion: external thoughts placed into the patient's mind. Thought broadcast: patient's thoughts transmitted/broadcast to others. Both are Schneiderian first rank symptoms involving disrupted ownership of thoughts. Reference: Schneider K. Clinical Psychopathology. 1959; Oyebode F. Sims' Symptoms in the Mind (5th ed.), 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of Schneider's first rank symptoms of schizophrenia?

options.text: Third-person auditory hallucinations (voices discussing the patient)

questions.explanation: Command hallucinations are NOT a Schneiderian first rank symptom. FRS include: third-person hallucinations, running commentary, thought echo, thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcast, passivity phenomena (made feelings, impulses, actions), somatic passivity, and delusional perception. Reference: Schneider K. Clinical Psychopathology, 1959.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is characteristic of attenuated psychosis syndrome (ultra-high risk state)?

options.text: Florid delusions of persecution with complete conviction
Attenuated psychotic symptoms including magical thinking and perceptual disturbances below threshold
Negative symptoms only, with no positive symptoms

correct_answer.text: Attenuated psychotic symptoms including magical thinking and perceptual disturbances below threshold

questions.explanation: Attenuated psychosis syndrome features sub-threshold psychotic symptoms: magical thinking, ideas of reference, perceptual disturbances, with retained insight. These are detectable in the prodromal period before first-episode psychosis. Reference: Yung AR et al. Acta Psychiatr Scand 1998;98:191-197.

questions.question_text: Which feature is specific to Complex PTSD (ICD-11) and distinguishes it from PTSD?

options.text: Negative alterations in cognition and mood

questions.explanation: ICD-11 Complex PTSD includes core PTSD symptoms PLUS three 'disturbances in self-organisation': affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and disturbances in relationships. It arises from prolonged, repeated trauma. Reference: Maercker A et al. Acta Psychiatr Scand 2013;128:198-207. ICD-11.

questions.question_text: Which medication has specific evidence for reducing nightmare frequency in PTSD?
questions.explanation: Prazosin (alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist) has evidence for reducing trauma-related nightmares in PTSD. It blocks central alpha-1 receptors to reduce noradrenergic hyperactivity during REM sleep. Reference: Raskind MA et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2002;63:565-568.

questions.question_text: A patient assigned male at birth identifies as a woman and has always felt her gender identity is female. Which term most accurately describes her identity?
questions.explanation: Transgender is an umbrella term for individuals whose gender identity differs from their sex assigned at birth. Cisgender means gender identity aligns with assigned sex. ICD-11 uses 'gender incongruence' as the diagnostic category. Reference: ICD-11 (HA60); APA Practice Guidelines.

questions.question_text: A patient hears a voice only when water is running from a tap. When no tap runs, no voice is heard. Both the tap sound and the voice are auditory. What is this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: A functional hallucination is triggered by a real external stimulus in the same sensory modality — both coexist simultaneously. Here the auditory tap sound triggers an auditory hallucination (voice). It differs from reflex hallucination (different modalities) and synaesthesia (non-pathological). Reference: Oyebode F. Sims' Symptoms in the Mind (5th ed.), 2015.

questions.question_text: A patient describes seeing a perfect mirror image of himself standing in front of him. He knows it is not real but finds it disturbing. Which perceptual phenomenon is this?
questions.explanation: Autoscopy is seeing one's own image (double/phantom) in external space appearing as a mirror reflection, observed from the person's normal bodily position. It is associated with temporal-parietal junction dysfunction. Reference: Blanke O, Mohr C. Brain Res Rev 2005;50:184-199.

questions.question_text: A patient with temporal lobe epilepsy describes floating above her body and seeing herself lying below. She maintains a sense of single identity located above. What is this experience?
questions.explanation: An out of body experience (OBE) involves perceiving oneself from an external elevated vantage point outside the physical body. OBEs occur in cardiac arrest, temporal-parietal junction stimulation, TLE, and near-death experiences. Reference: Blanke O et al. Nature 2002;419:269-270.

questions.question_text: A patient sees a teacup appear to remain frozen in her visual field for several seconds after looking away from it. Which perceptual abnormality does this describe?
questions.explanation: Palinopsia is persistence or recurrence of a visual image after the stimulus has ceased. It occurs in temporal/occipital lobe disorders, migraine, epilepsy, and as a side effect of trazodone and topiramate. Reference: Bender MB et al. Brain 1968;91:321-338.

questions.question_text: At a noisy party, a person simultaneously monitors other conversations and attends immediately when their name is mentioned. Which cognitive phenomenon does this demonstrate?

options.text: Selective auditory attention (the cocktail party effect)

correct_answer.text: Selective auditory attention (the cocktail party effect)

questions.explanation: The cocktail party effect (Cherry 1953) demonstrates selective auditory attention — the ability to extract a specific voice from noise while monitoring other streams for personally relevant signals. Impaired in schizophrenia, ADHD, and delirium. Reference: Cherry EC. J Acoust Soc Am 1953;25:975-979. Here is Part 3 (Questions 81 to 120) of the exam, with the Extended Matching Items (EMIs) converted into standalone multiple-choice questions with all options listed for each.

questions.question_text: A patient awakens from sleep with vivid, frightening dreams and full recall of the dream content. Which sleep disorder is most consistent?
questions.explanation: Nightmare disorder: frightening dreams (REM sleep, second half of night) with full recall upon awakening, rapid return to alertness. First-line: imagery rehearsal therapy (IRT), prazosin for PTSD-related nightmares. Reference: DSM-5, ICSD-3.

questions.question_text: A patient presents 12 hours after Substance dose use with agitation, lacrimation, and repeated yawning. Which withdrawal syndrome is characterised by yawning as a prominent feature?
questions.explanation: Yawning is a classic feature of opioid withdrawal, reflecting rebound noradrenergic hyperactivity from the locus coeruleus. Other features: lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, diaphoresis, mydriasis, myalgia. Reference: Kosten TR, Baxter LE. Am J Addict 2019;28:55-62.

questions.question_text: Which hormone, produced by adipose tissue, signals energy stores to the hypothalamus and reduces appetite?
questions.explanation: Leptin is produced by white adipose tissue proportional to fat mass. It signals energy sufficiency to the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, suppressing appetite (inhibiting NPY/AgRP neurons, stimulating POMC/CART). Leptin resistance characterises obesity. Reference: Friedman JM. Nat Metab 2019;1:754-764.

questions.question_text: Which hormone is produced from the intestine (duodenum and jejunum) in response to meals and reduces appetite?
questions.explanation: CCK is produced by I-cells in the duodenum/jejunum in response to fats and proteins. It reduces appetite by acting on CCK-A receptors (slowing gastric emptying) and CCK-B receptors in the brain. Ghrelin (stomach) is the primary hunger hormone. Reference: Chandra R, Liddle RA. Curr Opin Endocrinol Diabetes Obes 2007;14:63-67.

questions.question_text: A patient on venlafaxine and tramadol develops agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia, and lower limb clonus. Which feature is most specific for serotonin syndrome?
questions.explanation: Clonus (inducible lower limb clonus) is the most specific sign of serotonin syndrome per the Hunter Criteria. It reflects excess serotonergic activity in spinal cord 5-HT receptors. Distinguishes SS from NMS (which has lead-pipe rigidity). Reference: Boyer EW, Shannon M. N Engl J Med 2005;352:1112-1120.

questions.question_text: A researcher studies 17,000 adults attending a health check-up, divides them into four age groups, and asks them to recall childhood experiences. No follow-up is planned. Which study design is this?
questions.explanation: A cross-sectional study collects data from a population at a single point in time (a 'snapshot'). All data collection is at one time point, with no follow-up. Cross-sectional studies can establish prevalence and associations but cannot establish causality. Reference: Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research (4th ed.), 2013.

questions.question_text: A clinical psychologist needs a self-rated (patient-completed) depression scale rather than a clinician-administered scale. Which of the following is self-rated?

options.text: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia

questions.explanation: The BDI (BDI-II) is a 21-item self-report questionnaire. HAM-D and MADRS are clinician-administered. PHQ-9 and QIDS-SR are also self-rated. Reference: Beck AT et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1961;4:561-571.

questions.question_text: Which rating scale is specifically designed to assess the severity of psychotic symptoms across multiple domains including positive and negative symptoms?
questions.explanation: The BPRS is a clinician-rated scale assessing severity of psychotic symptoms and general psychopathology (positive, negative, and affective symptoms). PANSS is a more comprehensive alternative. Reference: Overall JE, Gorham DR. Psychol Rep 1962;10:799-812.

questions.question_text: Which antipsychotic is primarily excreted unchanged in the urine, making dose adjustment particularly important in renal failure?
questions.explanation: Sulpiride is excreted largely unchanged in the urine (~70% renal excretion), unlike most antipsychotics that undergo extensive hepatic metabolism. Dose reduction is required in renal impairment. Reference: Taylor D et al. Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (14th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: In which condition is lyonisation (X-inactivation) particularly clinically relevant in males?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) — males have two X chromosomes, so lyonisation inactivates one X in each cell (forming a Barr body). The pattern of inactivation can influence phenotypic severity. Reference: Lyon MF. Nature 1961;190:372-373.

questions.question_text: Southern blotting is used to detect which of the following?

options.text: Specific DNA sequences (detecting and sizing DNA fragments)

correct_answer.text: Specific DNA sequences (detecting and sizing DNA fragments)

questions.explanation: Southern blotting (Southern, 1975) detects specific DNA sequences. Steps: restriction enzyme digestion, gel electrophoresis, membrane transfer, hybridisation with labelled probe. Uses: gene mutations, RFLPs, CAG repeat expansions. Northern = RNA; Western = proteins. Reference: Southern EM. J Mol Biol 1975;98:503-517.

questions.question_text: A patient cannot recognise familiar faces despite intact visual acuity. Which brain area is most specifically associated with this deficit?

options.text: Fusiform face area (fusiform gyrus, occipitotemporal cortex)

correct_answer.text: Fusiform face area (fusiform gyrus, occipitotemporal cortex)

questions.explanation: Prosopagnosia (face blindness) is associated with damage to the fusiform face area (FFA, fusiform gyrus, BA37). The FFA shows selective activation to faces on fMRI and is damaged in acquired prosopagnosia. Reference: Kanwisher N et al. J Neurosci 1997;17:4302-4311.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best example of an idiosyncratic adverse drug reaction?

options.text: Dry mouth from a tricyclic antidepressant

questions.explanation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome from carbamazepine is an idiosyncratic (unpredictable, dose-independent, immunologically mediated) adverse reaction occurring in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-B*1502). All other options are predictable pharmacological effects. Reference: Edwards IR, Aronson JK. Lancet 2000;356:1255-1259.

questions.question_text: According to DSM-5, which is the minimum requirement for a diagnosis of Bipolar I disorder?

options.text: At least one manic episode and at least one major depressive episode
At least one manic episode (which may or may not be accompanied by depression)
At least two hypomanic episodes and one major depressive episode
At least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode
Three or more mood episodes including at least one depressive and one manic

correct_answer.text: At least one manic episode (which may or may not be accompanied by depression)

questions.explanation: DSM-5 Bipolar I requires at least one lifetime manic episode (duration ≥7 days, or any duration if hospitalisation required). A major depressive episode is NOT required. Bipolar II requires hypomania AND depression. Reference: DSM-5, APA, 2013.

questions.question_text: In ICD-11, which major psychiatric disorder lacks the Type I/Type II subdivision used in DSM-5?
questions.explanation: In ICD-11, Bipolar disorder is classified with Bipolar type I and II, but the distinction is less emphasised than in DSM-5, which clearly separates Bipolar I (≥1 manic episode) from Bipolar II (hypomania + depression, no mania). Reference: ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics (2022).

questions.question_text: A patient demonstrates dyscalculia, dysgraphia, left-right disorientation, and finger agnosia. Which syndrome is present and where is the lesion?

options.text: Gerstmann syndrome – dominant parietal lobe (angular gyrus, inferior parietal lobule)
Anton syndrome – bilateral occipital lobe lesions

correct_answer.text: Gerstmann syndrome – dominant parietal lobe (angular gyrus, inferior parietal lobule)

questions.explanation: Gerstmann syndrome (tetrad: dyscalculia, dysgraphia, left-right disorientation, finger agnosia) localises to the dominant parietal lobe (angular gyrus, BA39). Reference: Gerstmann J. 1924; Rusconi E et al. Cortex 2010;20:8723.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive deficit is the core, defining feature of delirium that distinguishes it from dementia?

options.text: Impaired attention (disturbance in attention and awareness)

correct_answer.text: Impaired attention (disturbance in attention and awareness)

questions.explanation: Impaired attention and awareness is the core defining feature of delirium (DSM-5 and ICD-11). Dementia causes multiple cognitive deficits but attention is relatively preserved until late stages. CAM uses inattention as a core criterion. Reference: DSM-5; NICE Delirium Guideline (CG103), 2010.

questions.question_text: Approximately what percentage of children exposed to valproate in utero will develop a neurodevelopmental disorder?
questions.explanation: Approximately 30-40% of children exposed to valproate in utero develop a neurodevelopmental disorder (ASD, intellectual disability, ADHD). Additionally ~10% have major congenital malformations. Valproate is contraindicated in women who could become pregnant. Reference: MHRA Drug Safety Update 2018; Bromley R et al. Neurotoxicol Teratol 2010;32:363-369.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines stupor in psychiatric phenomenology?

options.text: A state of impaired consciousness on the continuum between drowsiness and coma
A combination of akinetism (immobility) and mutism, with preserved consciousness
Profound depressive withdrawal with complete self-neglect but maintained voluntary movement
A state of complete unresponsiveness to all external stimuli, equivalent to coma
Intermittent loss of consciousness associated with tonic-clonic movements

correct_answer.text: A combination of akinetism (immobility) and mutism, with preserved consciousness

questions.explanation: Psychiatric stupor (Jaspers, Oyebode) is defined as a combination of akinetism (absence of voluntary movement) and mutism, with preserved consciousness. The patient is aware but cannot act or speak. Occurs in catatonic schizophrenia, depressive and manic stupor, and dissociative states. Reference: Oyebode F. Sims' Symptoms in the Mind (5th ed.), 2015. Theme: Mechanisms of Action of Substances of Misuse

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old is brought to A&E after snorting a white powder. He is euphoric, tachycardic, and hypertensive. Neuroimaging shows reduced DAT binding in the striatum. Which mechanism best explains the euphoric effects?

options.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine
Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores
Agonism at 5-HT2A receptors in cortical pyramidal neurons
Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors
Agonism at CB1 and CB2 endocannabinoid receptors

correct_answer.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine

questions.explanation: Cocaine blocks the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), accumulating dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. Unlike amphetamine, it does not cause active dopamine release from vesicular stores. Reference: Stahl SM, Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology (5th ed.), 2021.

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old uses a substance before exams. He describes intense rush and reduced appetite. The substance causes active efflux of dopamine from presynaptic terminals rather than simply blocking reuptake. Which mechanism?

options.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine
Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores
Agonism at 5-HT2A receptors in cortical pyramidal neurons
Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors
Agonism at CB1 and CB2 endocannabinoid receptors

correct_answer.text: Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores

questions.explanation: Amphetamine reverses the DAT causing dopamine efflux and displaces dopamine from vesicular storage via VMAT2 inhibition. This active release mechanism produces higher synaptic dopamine than cocaine. Reference: Nestler EJ. Molecular Neuropharmacology (3rd ed.), 2015.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old has taken a substance producing profound perceptual distortions and ego dissolution. These effects are blocked by ketanserin. What is the primary mechanism?

options.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine
Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores
Agonism at 5-HT2A receptors in cortical pyramidal neurons
Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors
Agonism at CB1 and CB2 endocannabinoid receptors

correct_answer.text: Agonism at 5-HT2A receptors in cortical pyramidal neurons

questions.explanation: Psilocybin (converted to psilocin) acts as a partial agonist at 5-HT2A receptors in cortical pyramidal neurons. Ketanserin (5-HT2A antagonist) reverses these effects. All classical psychedelics act via 5-HT2A agonism. Reference: Nichols DE. Pharmacol Rev 2016;68:264-355.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old consumes several cups of a beverage and feels more alert. The substance blocks a receptor that normally promotes sleepiness as it accumulates during wakefulness. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine
Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores
Agonism at 5-HT2A receptors in cortical pyramidal neurons
Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors
Agonism at CB1 and CB2 endocannabinoid receptors

correct_answer.text: Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors

questions.explanation: Caffeine competitively antagonises adenosine A1 and A2A receptors. Adenosine accumulates during wakefulness and promotes sleep; blocking it promotes alertness. Reference: Fredholm BB et al. Pharmacol Rev 1999;51:83-133.

questions.question_text: A patient uses a herbal substance regularly and reports a relaxed euphoric state with altered time perception. The active compound mimics an endogenous lipid signalling system. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Blockade of the dopamine reuptake transporter (DAT), increasing synaptic dopamine
Reversal of the dopamine transporter and release of dopamine from vesicular stores
Agonism at 5-HT2A receptors in cortical pyramidal neurons
Competitive antagonism at adenosine A1 and A2A receptors
Agonism at CB1 and CB2 endocannabinoid receptors

correct_answer.text: Agonism at CB1 and CB2 endocannabinoid receptors

questions.explanation: Cannabis (THC) acts as a partial agonist at CB1 and CB2 endocannabinoid receptors. CB1 receptors are widely expressed in the brain. The endogenous ligands are anandamide and 2-AG. Reference: Mechoulam R, Parker LA. Annu Rev Psychol 2013;64:21-47. Theme: Mechanisms of Action of Psychiatric Medications

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist prescribes an antidepressant that helps a patient with comorbid nicotine dependence. It is not an SSRI and does not significantly affect serotonin reuptake. It is associated with lowering seizure threshold. What is its mechanism?

options.text: Non-competitive antagonism at NMDA glutamate receptors
Competitive antagonism at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors
Partial agonism at mu-opioid receptors and antagonism at kappa-opioid receptors

questions.explanation: Bupropion is a norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) with minimal serotonin activity. Its dopaminergic mechanism supports smoking cessation. It lowers seizure threshold above 450mg/day. Reference: Stahl SM et al. J Clin Psychiatry 2004;65:182-192.

questions.question_text: An old age psychiatrist prescribes a medication for moderate Alzheimer's that reduces excitotoxic neuronal damage by blocking pathological chronic glutamate receptor activation while preserving normal phasic signalling. What is its mechanism?

options.text: Non-competitive antagonism at NMDA glutamate receptors
Competitive antagonism at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors
Partial agonism at mu-opioid receptors and antagonism at kappa-opioid receptors

correct_answer.text: Non-competitive antagonism at NMDA glutamate receptors

questions.explanation: Memantine is a non-competitive NMDA antagonist that preferentially blocks tonically over-activated receptors (reducing excitotoxicity) while sparing physiological phasic activation needed for memory. Reference: Lipton SA. Nature Rev Drug Discov 2006;5:160-170.

questions.question_text: A patient is brought to A&E after combined benzodiazepine and zopiclone overdose. The physician administers an IV agent that reverses sedation by acting at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors. Which mechanism?

options.text: Non-competitive antagonism at NMDA glutamate receptors
Competitive antagonism at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors
Partial agonism at mu-opioid receptors and antagonism at kappa-opioid receptors

correct_answer.text: Competitive antagonism at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors

questions.explanation: Flumazenil competitively antagonises benzodiazepines and zopiclone at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors, reversing sedation. Reference: BNF. Rang HP et al. Pharmacology (9th ed.), 2019.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 4-year-old son who enthusiastically plans play activities but becomes very upset and self-critical when reprimanded. According to Erikson\'s theory, which developmental stage is he navigating?
questions.explanation: A 4-year-old is in Erikson\'s Initiative vs Guilt stage (3-6 years). Children assert themselves and initiate activities; failure leads to excessive guilt. Key virtue: purpose. Reference: Erikson EH. Childhood and Society. Norton, 1950.

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old works diligently at school, takes pride in completing projects, and competes with classmates for achievement. She becomes distressed when she perceives herself as less competent. Which Eriksonian stage describes her?

options.text: Autonomy vs shame and doubt (Erikson, 18 months–3 years)

questions.explanation: Industry vs inferiority (6-12 years): children develop competence through mastering academic and social skills. Failure leads to feelings of inferiority. Reference: Erikson EH. Childhood and Society. Norton, 1950.

questions.question_text: A 3-month-old infant's primary developmental task involves developing a fundamental sense of confidence that the world is safe and caregivers will meet their needs. Which Eriksonian stage is this?

options.text: Autonomy vs shame and doubt (Erikson, 18 months–3 years)

questions.explanation: Trust vs Mistrust (0-18 months): consistent, sensitive caregiving leads to trust (key virtue: hope); neglect or inconsistency leads to mistrust. Reference: Erikson EH. Childhood and Society. Norton, 1950. Theme: Types of Memory

questions.question_text: A patient with temporal lobe damage cannot recall what he had for breakfast, nor remember his grandson's birthday party last week. His neuropsychologist explains this reflects impairment of a memory system storing personally experienced events with spatiotemporal context. Which type?
questions.explanation: Episodic memory stores personally experienced events with their spatiotemporal context. It is highly vulnerable to hippocampal damage and impaired early in Alzheimer's. Reference: Tulving E. Annu Rev Psychol 2002;53:1-25.

questions.question_text: A patient with severe anterograde amnesia accurately defines words, explains general knowledge facts, and identifies famous people. This preserved knowledge exists independently of personal experience. Which type?
questions.explanation: Semantic memory stores general world knowledge — facts, concepts, word meanings — independent of personal experience. It is more resistant to hippocampal damage than episodic memory. Reference: Tulving E, Markowitsch HJ. Hippocampus 1998;8:198-204.

questions.question_text: A patient remembers to telephone their GP next Monday at 10am, as requested during their last appointment. This memory involves remembering to perform an intended action at a future time. What type?
questions.explanation: Prospective memory involves remembering to perform planned actions at a future time (time-based) or upon a specific cue (event-based). It is impaired in depression, schizophrenia, and frontal lobe disorders. Reference: McDaniel MA, Einstein GO. Prospective Memory, 2007.

questions.question_text: Despite severe amnesia preventing new fact learning, a patient with Korsakoff syndrome can still play piano at a high level learned before his illness. He has no conscious recall of learning to play. Which memory is preserved?
questions.explanation: Procedural memory stores motor skills, habits, and learned procedures (riding a bike, playing piano). It is implicit (no conscious recall required), stored in basal ganglia and cerebellum, and preserved in hippocampal amnesia. Reference: Squire LR. Neurobiol Learn Mem 2004;82:171-177.

questions.question_text: A trainee asks a patient to repeat digits of increasing length forward and backward. This test measures temporary storage and manipulation of information 'online' during cognitive tasks. Which memory system is being assessed?
questions.explanation: Working memory (Baddeley's model) temporarily stores and manipulates information for ongoing cognitive tasks. Digit span assesses the phonological loop. It is impaired in schizophrenia, ADHD, and frontal lobe disorders. Reference: Baddeley AD. Working Memory, 1986. Would you like me to proceed with the final batch (Questions 121 to 150)?
